At height z, the horizontal triangle has half-width L1−z/(2H)​ along x and depth D(1−z/H) along y. These shrink with z, so its orthogonal projection onto the (x,y) plane is the base triangle with vertices (−L,0), (L,0) and (0,D):
0≤y≤D,∣x∣≤L(1−y/D).
(33)
The orthogonal projection onto the (y,z) plane is the triangle with vertices (0,0), (D,0) and (0,H):
0≤z≤H,0≤y≤D(1−z/H).
(34)
The orthogonal projection onto the (x,z) plane is bounded by z=0, z=H and the two curves
x=±L1−z/(2H)​,0≤z≤H.​
(35)
Equivalently, these curves lie on the parabola z=2H(1−x2/L2), truncated at height H. In particular the top width is 2​L, so this projection has a horizontal upper edge from −L/2​ to L/2​; it is not triangular. The top horizontal cross-section has zero depth, consistent with this edge.

a OurBigBook.com
On an interval with x=0, division by x2 gives the separable differential equation y′=(4/x2−1/x)y2. For y=0, take antiderivatives:
∫y2dy​=∫(x24​−x1​)dx,−y1​=−x4​−ln∣x∣+C.
(39)
Renaming the constant yields the explicit nonzero family
y(x)=4/x+ln∣x∣+C1​.​
(40)
For x=0, the interval of definition must avoid zeros of the denominator. Division by y2 excluded the additional solution y(x)≡0​, which must also be included.
The original undivided differential equation also makes sense at x=0, where it requires y(0)=0. For continuation through a zero of the leading ODE coefficient, rewrite the nonzero family as
y(x)=4+xln∣x∣+Cxx​.
(41)
It extends differentiably with y(0)=0 and y′(0)=1/4, since y(x)/x→1/4. One may choose the integration constants independently on the two sides of zero and obtain a differentiable solution through zero. The zero solution also extends through zero, with derivative 0; joining a nonzero branch on just one side to a zero branch on the other would fail differentiability.

y(x)=cosxsinx+2​​,−2π​<x<2π​.​

Use the substitution v=y/x for a homogeneous first-order differential equation. Since y′=v+xv′, it gives
xv′=tanv.
(44)
Where sinv=0, this separable differential equation integrates to ln∣sinv∣=ln∣x∣+C, hence sinv=C1​x. One can obtain the same relation without division by sinv: the equation gives (sinv)′=(sinv)/x, so sinv=C1​x, including sinv≡0.
All real branches of the inverse sine are captured by
y(x)=x[kπ+(−1)karcsin(Cx)],C∈R,k∈Z.​
(45)
Each branch is used on an interval with x=0 and ∣Cx∣<1, with fixed k. The strict inequality excludes zeros of cos(y/x), where the original tangent is undefined. When C=0, the formula includes all straight-line solutions y=kπx. Keeping both families of inverse sine branches is essential for the two different initial conditions below.

For an exact differential form, equality of the mixed partial derivatives requires Py​=Qx​. Here
Py​=ax​1+y2​y​,Qx​=2x​1+y2​y​.
(48)
Equality for all x>0 and real y forces 1/a=1/2, so a=2​. To construct the potential, integrate P with respect to x:
v(x,y)=x​(1+1+y2​)+C(y).
(49)
Differentiation with respect to y gives vy​=Q+C′(y), so C′(y)=0. Thus the most general potential on the connected domain x>0 is
v(x,y)=x​(1+1+y2​)+C,C∈R.​
(50)
Its explicit partial derivatives verify sufficiency as well as necessity.

b OurBigBook.com
The stated total differential is that of πr2h, so V=πr2h+C. The zero-volume condition gives C=0. For positive r,h, divide the total differential by this volume to obtain
VdV​=2rdr​+hdh​.​
(51)
For the specified small changes, dV/V≈2(0.01)+0.02=0.04, so the volume increases by approximately 4%. The fractional expression requires V>0; at a degenerate zero-volume state it is undefined. For finite changes, the exact multiplier is (1.01)2(1.02), whose difference from 1 is 4.0502%; the total differential gives its first-order approximation.

ux​=ϕ(t)+xϕ′(t)(−x2y​)=ϕ(t)−tϕ′(t),uy​=xϕ′(t)x1​=ϕ′(t).

The chain rule expresses the coordinate differential operators as

The coefficients are constant, so a second application gives
uxx​=a2uξξ​+ab(uξη​+uηξ​)+b2uηη​,

L'Hôpital's rule applies to a quotient f(x)/g(x) of differentiable functions near a limiting point, excluding that point itself, provided g′(x)=0 there. If the quotient has an indeterminate form 0/0 or ∞/∞, and the limit of f′(x)/g′(x) exists as a finite or infinite value L, then
x→alim​g(x)f(x)​=x→alim​g′(x)f′(x)​=L.​
(92)
The rule also applies to one-sided limits and to limits at infinity, under the corresponding hypotheses. Existence of the derivative-ratio limit and the indeterminate-form hypotheses are required; an arbitrary quotient cannot be replaced by a quotient of derivatives.

a OurBigBook.com
For a differentiable objective f and regular constraint g=r, a constrained stationary point satisfies
∇f=λ∇g,g=r,​
(98)
where λ is a Lagrange multiplier. Solve these equations for both the coordinates and λ.
Geometrically, the gradient ∇g is normal to the constraint level set when ∇g=0. Every feasible infinitesimal displacement v is tangent to that level set, so ∇g⋅v=0. At a constrained stationary point, the directional change ∇f⋅v must also vanish for every such tangent displacement. Thus ∇f is normal to the same tangent plane and is a scalar multiple of ∇g. This is the geometric basis of the Lagrange multiplier method.
For a second constraint h=s, with linearly independent vectors ∇g and ∇h, the feasible tangent directions are perpendicular to both. Their normal space is the linear span of these two gradients, so introduce a second Lagrange multiplier:
∇f=λ∇g+μ∇h,g=r,h=s.​
(99)
These equations find candidates; deciding whether they are maxima, minima or saddle points requires further analysis. Constraint points where the required gradient independence fails must be examined separately.

The angles in the PDF are measured from the vertical normal to the interface. The horizontal displacements of the two path segments are d1​tanθ and d2​tanϕ, while their lengths are d1​secθ and d2​secϕ. Thus the geometric constraint and travel time are
g(θ,ϕ)=d1​tanθ+d2​tanϕ=D,T(θ,ϕ)=c2d1​secθ+2​d2​secϕ​.
(100)
The Lagrange multiplier equations ∇T=λ∇g give
c2d1​​secθtanθ=λd1​sec2θ,c2​d2​​secϕtanϕ=λd2​sec2ϕ.
(101)
Cancelling the positive geometric factors gives λ=2sinθ/c=2​sinϕ/c, hence
sinϕ=2​sinθ.​
(102)
This is Snell's law, sinθ/(c/2)=sinϕ/(c/2​). The relation depends only on the ratio of the two speeds, so changing D,d1​,d2​ leaves the relation unchanged; it changes which angles satisfy it together with the geometric constraint.
For a minimum check, let u be the horizontal distance to the crossing point. Then
T(u)=c2​u2+d12​​+c2​​(D−u)2+d22​​,
(103)
and
T′′(u)=c(u2+d12​)3/22d12​​+c((D−u)2+d22​)3/22​d22​​>0.
(104)
Thus the travel time is a strictly convex function of u, and its stationary point is the unique global minimum. For positive D,d1​,d2​, T′(0)<0<T′(D), placing the crossing between the two endpoint projections.
